                                                            Permanence of Weakly Reversible Mass-Action Systems
                                                                        with a Single Linkage Class∗
                                                                               Balázs Boros† and Josef Hofbauer‡


                                           Abstract. We give a new proof of the fact that each weakly reversible mass-action system with a single linkage
                                                     class is permanent.

                                           Key words. mass-action system, entropy, permanence




arXiv:1903.03071v2 [math.DS] 13 Mar 2019
                                           AMS subject classifications. 34C11, 34D23, 80A30, 92E20

                                                1. Introduction. Horn and Jackson [15] considered the class of weakly reversible mass-
                                           action systems and they showed that complex balanced equilibria are unique and asymptot-
                                           ically stable relative to their positive stoichiometric class by providing a global Lyapunov
                                           function. However, existence of complex balanced equilibria is a rare situation. On the other
                                           hand, every weakly reversible mass-action system has a positive equilibrium in each positive
                                           stoichiometric class [4]. In general, little can be said about the number of equilibria and
                                           their stability. It is natural to ask whether other (more global) dynamical properties hold for
                                           weakly reversible mass-action systems. For example whether all species coexist for all times
                                           and their concentrations remain bounded. These ideas have been formalized as the concepts
                                           of persistence, boundedness, and permanence, and several conjectures have been formulated
                                           for weakly reversible (and even more general classes, like endotactic) mass-action systems, see
                                           e.g. [7], [2], [1], [8], [16], [12], [13], and [3]. Many of these papers use the classical, entropy-
                                           like Lyapunov function by Horn and Jackson. In particular, Anderson shows persistence and
                                           boundedness for weakly reversible mass-action systems with a single linkage class (see [2] and
                                           [1]), Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu extend this to show permanence for the even larger class
                                           of strongly endotactic mass-action systems (see [12] and [13]), and Anderson, Cappelletti,
                                           Kim, and Nguyen give further insight (see [3]).
                                                In the present paper, we provide a new proof for the permanence of weakly reversible
                                           mass-action systems with a single linkage class. We simplify the previous approaches, and
                                           give a more concise and elementary proof of the fact that a variant of the classical Horn-
                                           Jackson function is a Lyapunov function near the boundary of the state space. We crucially
                                           use ideas from [9] and [4]. On the other hand, we demonstrate in section 7 that the method
                                           breaks down for weakly reversible networks with multiple linkage classes.
                                                The rest of this paper is organized as follows. After introducing some notations and
                                           the necessary notions from chemical reaction network theory (CRNT) in sections 2 and 3,
                                           respectively, we state the main result of this paper in section 4. We collect a series of lemmata
                                              ∗

in section 5 and prove the main result in section 6. We illustrate the limitations of the method
in section 7. Finally, we display in Appendix A the dependency of the statements in sections 4
and 5 via an acyclic digraph.
     2. Notations. We use standard notations.
     The symbols R+ and R≥0 denote the sets of positive and nonnegative real numbers, respec-
tively. Accordingly, Rn+ and Rn≥0 denote the positive and nonnegative orthants, respectively.
                               n            n                 y
Qn Forysthe vectors x ∈ R+ and y ∈ R , the notation x is a shorthand for the monomial
   s=1 xs .
     For a vector z ∈ Rm , the smallest and largest value among the coordinates of z are denoted
by min z and max z, respectively.
     For a vector x ∈ Rn and a subset W of {1, . . . , n}, the vector xW ∈ RW is the restriction
of x to the indices in W .
     For a set W ⊆ {1, . . . , n}, we denote by W c the set {1, . . . , n} \ W .
     For a set A ⊆ Rn , the symbols A and ∂A denote the closure and the boundary of A,
respectively.
     3. Mass-action systems. We give a very brief introduction to the basic notions of CRNT.
For more details, the reader is advised to consult e.g. [10], [11], and [14].
     A reaction network is a triple (X , C, R), where X , C, and R are the set of species, complexes,
and reactions, respectively. Throughout the paper, we use n = |X | and m = |C|. The
complexes are formal linear combinations of the species, the coefficients are stored in the
matrix Y = [y1 , . . . , ym ] ∈ Rn×m . The ith complex is then (yi )1 X1 + · · · + (yi )n Xn , where
X1 , . . . , Xn denote the species. The set R consists of ordered pairs of complexes, the first and
the second element of the pair are called reactant complex and product complex, respectively.
     The weak components of the digraph (C, R) are called linkage classes. The reaction
network is said to be weakly reversible if all the weak components of the digraph (C, R) are
strongly connected, i.e., for every pair (i, j) of complexes, the existence of a directed path
from i to j implies the existence of a directed path from j to i. Most of the results in this
paper are about weakly reversible networks with a single linkage class, i.e., the digraph (C, R)
is strongly connected. When having a single linkage class network, usually it is required that
there are at least two complexes and all the complexes are distinct. However, we assume only
that there exist at least two complexes that are distinct (thus, there might be i, j ∈ {1, . . . , m}
such that i 6= j and yi = yj ). We make this weakening for convenience.
     Denoting by x(τ ) ∈ Rn+ the concentration vector of the species at time τ , assuming mass-
action kinetics, the time evolution of the species concentration vector is described by the
autonomous ordinary differential equation (ODE)
                                 X
                     ẋ(τ ) =             κij x(τ )yi (yj − yi ) with state space Rn+ ,
                                (i,j)∈R


where κ : R → R+ . The reason we defined the ODE in the positive orthant (not in the
nonnegative orthant) is that we allow negative entries in Y . The quadruple (X , C, R, κ) is
called a mass-action system.
    In fact, we will consider a slightly more general family of differential equations. Namely,
PERMANENCE OF MASS-ACTION SYSTEMS                                                               3


the non-autonomous ODE
                               X
(3.1)              ẋ(τ ) =             κij (τ )x(τ )yi (yj − yi ) with state space Rn+ ,
                              (i,j)∈R


with an 0 < ε < 1 such that ε ≤ κij (τ ) ≤ 1/ε for all (i, j) ∈ R and for all τ ≥ 0. The
quadruple (X , C, R, κ(τ )) is called a mass-action system with bounded kinetics.
    The linear subspace S of Rn+ , spanned by the set {yi − yj | (i, j) ∈ R}, is called the
stoichiometric subspace. Clearly, the translations of S are forward invariant under the ODE
(3.1). The sets (p + S) ∩ Rn+ for p ∈ Rn+ are called positive stoichiometric classes. The relevant
approach is to study the dynamics within a fixed positive stoichometric class.

    4. Main result. The formal definition of permanence is the following.
    Definition 4.1. A mass-action system with bounded kinetics is said to be permanent on the
positive stoichiometric class P if there exists a compact set K ⊆ P with the property that for
each solution τ 7→ x(τ ) with x(0) ∈ P, there exists a τ0 ≥ 0 such that for all τ ≥ τ0 we have
x(τ ) ∈ K.
    Results on permanence of planar systems include [17], [8], [6], and [5], while in the papers
[1] and [13] there is no restriction on the number of species. The Permanence Conjecture
states that all weakly reversible mass-action systems with bounded kinetics are permanent
in each positive stoichiometric class. In [12] and [13], the conjecture is proven in the single
linkage class case, see [13, Theorem 1.3], and the same result follows from [3, Theorem 5.5] in
case the rate constants do not depend on time. In this paper, we give a more concise proof of
the single linkage class case of the conjecture.
    Next, we state our main result as Theorem 4.2. Its proof is carried out in section 6, after
collecting a series of lemmata in section 5.
    Theorem 4.2. Let (X , C, R, κ(τ )) be a weakly reversible, single linkage class mass-action
system with bounded kinetics. Fix a positive stoichiometric class P. Then
    (i) there exists a compact and forward invariant set K ⊆ P with the property that each
        solution starting in P enters K in finite time and
   (ii) the system, restricted to P, is permanent.
    By forward invariance in (i) of the above theorem, we mean that for all τ0 ≥ 0, x(τ0 ) ∈ K
implies x(τ ) ∈ K for all τ ≥ τ0 . Note that (i) immediately implies (ii). Furthermore, for
autonomous systems, (i) and (ii) are equivalent, because a compact set that all solutions
enter can be enlarged to a compact and forward invariant set. However, for non-autonomous
systems, (i) is a much stronger property than (ii).

    5. Lemmata. In this section, we collect a series of lemmata, the final two, Lemmata 5.7
and 5.8 will be used in section 6 to prove Theorem 4.2.

    The following lemma, despite its simplicity, plays a crucial role in the sequel. Several
versions appear in the CRNT literature, starting with [15, Lemma 4B]. See [4, Appendix A]
for a list of further appearances.
    Lemma 5.3. Let (X , C, R) be a reaction network and R′ ⊆ R be such that the set of vec-
tors {yj − yi | (i, j) ∈ R′ } forms a basis of S, hence, |R′ | = dim S. For a fixed positive
stoichiometric class P, let us define Ψ : P → Rdim
                                               +
                                                   S by

                                           yj 
                                           x

                                           xyi (i,j)∈R′

Then Ψ is a homeomorphism between P and Rdim
                                         +
                                             S.

                     yj
    Proof. Since xxyi = ehyj −yi ,log xi , the bijectivity of the map Ψ is equivalent to the bijectivity
of the map log ◦Ψ : P → Rdim S , and the latter is equivalent to the following statement. For
each x∗ ∈ Rn there exists a unique x ∈ P such that log x − log x∗ ∈ S ⊥ . The latter statement
is widely known to be true, and thus, the bijectivity of Ψ follows. It is also immediate that Ψ
is even a homeomorphism.
    Next, we prove that close enough to the boundary of a positive stoichiometric class, there
exists a monomial whose value is significantly smaller than the sum of the values of the other
monomials.

    We now prove that the classical Horn-Jackson function is a Lyapunov function around
infinity. Thus, we reprove [1, Theorem 3.12].

    In a similar way one can show that V is a Lyapunov function near the origin. For later
use, we prove a more general result. We show that appropriate variants of the classical Horn-
Jackson function are Lyapunov functions near the boundary of the positive orthant. This
latter fact appeared implicitly in [2] for weakly reversible mass-action systems with a single
linkage class and in [13] and [3] for the larger class of strongly endotactic mass-action systems.

    We conclude the proof similarly to the proof of Lemma 5.5 – with the subtle difference that
we consider the projected mass-action system. For the projected network, the set of species
is W , the set of complexes is {yW | y ∈ C}, and the set of reactions is R. Since W is not an
arbitrary nonempty subset of X , but the complement of the support of a point in P ∩ ∂Rn≥0 ,
cannot all the complexes in the projected network be identical. The rate constants of the
projected mass-action system are κ(τ ) as defined above. Although κ(τ ) is not necessarily
bounded away from zero and infinity for all τ ≥ 0, it is between two bounds whenever the
solution is close to x, and this is enough. Our goal is to show that VW serves as a Lyapunov
function around the origin for the projected mass-action system.
    In what follows, the index W refers to the corresponding quantity of the projected mass-
action system. Thus, PW is the positive stoichiometric class whose closure contains the
origin of RW . By applying Lemma 5.2, let δ > 0 be so small that g(τ, z(τ )) < 0 whenever
                                       dim PW
min z(τ ) ≤ δ. Let ΨW : PW → R+               be the homeomorphism in Lemma 5.3 and, by
applying Lemma 5.4, let M > 1 be so big that if x ∈ PW \ Ψ−1       W (UM ) then min z ≤ δ. To
conclude the proof, choose a neighborhood U of x in P such that |xs − xs | ≤ ω for all s ∈ W c
and the projection of U to the species W is disjoint from the compact set Ψ−1   W (UM ).
    The contents of next two lemmata are that the trajectories are uniformly bounded and
the origin is uniformly repelling, respectively. The proofs are analogous, we detail only the
second one.
     Lemma 5.7. Let (X , C, R, κ(τ )) be a weakly reversible, single linkage class mass-action
system with bounded kinetics and unbounded positive stoichiometric classes. Fix a positive
stoichiometric class P and let V : Rn≥0 → R≥0 be as in Lemma 5.5. For a c > n, let
U >c = {x ∈ P | V (x) > c} and U =c = {x ∈ P | V (x) = c}. Then there exists a c > n such
that

     (i) dτ V (x(τ )) < 0 whenever τ ≥ 0 is such that x(τ ) ∈ U >c ,
    (ii) the set P \ U >c is bounded and forward invariant,
   (iii) for all τ ≥ 0 with x(τ ) ∈ U >c , there exists a τ ′ ≥ τ such that x(τ ′ ) ∈ U =c .
     Lemma 5.8. Let (X , C, R, κ(τ )) be a weakly reversible, single linkage class mass-action
system with bounded kinetics. Consider the positive stoichiometric class P for which 0 ∈ P
(if such a P exists). Let V : Rn≥0 → R≥0 be as in Lemma 5.5. For a c ≥ 0, let

                          U >c = {x ∈ P | V (x) > c and max x ≤ 1},

     Proof. Since V has a local maximum at 0 and V (0) = n, the requirements (i) and (ii) are
satisfied for all c < n. If c < n is close enough to n then (iii) follows from Lemma 5.6. The
property (iv) follows immediately from (iii).
     To prove (v), let τ0 ≥ 0 with x(τ0 ) ∈ U >c , where c < n is such that (i), (ii), (iii), and
(iv) hold. Assume by contradiction that there exists an x ∈ P ∩ ∂Rn≥0 and τ0 ≤ τ1 < τ2 < · · ·
such that x(τk ) ∈ U >c converges to x as k → ∞. Let W = {s ∈ {1, . . . , n} | xs = 0}. W.l.o.g.,
choose the accumulation point x such that W is maximal. Note that W 6= {1, . . . , n} by (iii).
Since VW is continuous and VW (x) > VW (x) for all x ∈ U >c , we can choose a subsequence,
again denoted by (τk )k≥1 , such that VW (x(τk )) increases monotonically to VW (x) as k → ∞.
Then for each k ≥ 1 there exists a τk′ such that τk < τk′ < τk+1 , VW (x(τk )) ≤ VW (x(τk′ )) ≤

VW (x), and dτ   VW (x(τk′ )) ≥ 0. Now pick a subsequence, again denoted by (τk′ )k≥1 , such that

    ′

we have x′s = 0 if s ∈ W . In fact, because of the maximality of W , x′s = 0 if and only if

s ∈ W . By Lemma 5.6, applied to x′ , we get that dτ       VW (x(τk′ )) < 0 for large enough k, a

diction that for all τ ≥ τ0 we have x(τ ) ∈ U >c . Thus, the closure of the trajectory (x(τ ))τ ≥τ0 ,

    6. Proof of Theorem 4.2. In this section, we prove statement (i) of Theorem 4.2. As we
already mentioned, statement (ii) then follows immediately.
    Fix a positive stoichiometric class P. We will construct a compact and forward invari-
ant set K ⊆ P with the property that each solution starting in P enters K in finite time.
The boundary of P is composed of level set pieces of V and VW in Lemmata 5.5 and 5.6,
respectively.
    If P is unbounded, pick a c > n as in Lemma 5.7, and let U∞ = U >c . If P is bounded, let
U∞ = ∅.
    Pick a vertex x of P and let W = {s ∈ {1, . . . , n} | xs = 0}. Our goal is to define a set
UW ⊆ P with
     (i) UW is open relative to P,
    (ii) UW is a neighborhood of x in P,
   (iii) P \ UW is forward invariant.
   (iv) for all τ ≥ 0 with x(τ ) ∈ UW , there exists a τ ′ ≥ τ such that x(τ ′ ) ∈ P \ UW .
To this end, as in the proof of Lemma 5.8, we consider the projected mass-action system. For
the projected network, the set of species is W , the set of complexes is {yW | y ∈ C}, and the
set of reactions is R. Since W is not an arbitrary nonempty subset of X , but the complement
of the support of a point in P ∩ ∂Rn≥0 , not all the complexes in the projected network can
be identical. Let PW be the positive stoichiometric class in the projected network, whose
closure contains the origin of RW . The rate constants of the projected mass-action system
                                 i
are κij (τ ) = κij (τ )xW c (τ )yW c for (i, j) ∈ R. By Lemma 5.5, κ(τ ) is bounded away from
infinity. And, though κ(τ ) is not necessarily bounded away from zero, it is between two
bounds whenever the solution of the original system is close to x.
10                                                                    B. BOROS AND J. HOFBAUER


    Now apply Lemma 5.8 to the projected system and pick a c ≥ 0 such that U >c ⊆ PW has
the five properties in that lemma. Then the set UW = {x ∈ P | xW ∈ U >c } satisfies the four
requirements above.
    Denote by W0 the set of those W , which correspond to vertices of P. Let
                                                        
                                                 [
                                P1 = P \ U∞ ∪       UW  .
                                                     W ∈W0

    Pick now an edge e of P and let e = e∩P1 . Pick an x ∈ e and let W = {s ∈ {1, . . . , n} | xs =
0} (note that W does not depend on the choice of x). Our goal is to define a set UW ⊆ P
with
     (i) UW is open relative to P,
    (ii) UW is a neighborhood of e in P,
   (iii) P1 \ UW is forward invariant.
   (iv) for all τ ≥ 0 with x(τ ) ∈ UW , there exists a τ ′ ≥ τ such that x(τ ′ ) ∈ P1 \ UW .
To this end, we consider the projected mass-action system, similarly as above. In a neigh-
borhood of e, the rate constants of the projected mass-action system are bounded away from
zero, and thus, Lemma 5.8 applies to the projected system. Similarly as above, we get the set
UW that satisfies the four requirements.
    Denote by W1 the set of those W , which correspond to edges of P. Let
                                                           
                                                   [
                                    P2 = P1 \          UW  .
                                                  W ∈W1

    Continue this procedure with the two-dimensional faces of P to get P3 , etc. Finally, the
last step produces the compact and forward invariant set K = Pdim S in P that attracts every
solution in finite time. This concludes the proof of Theorem 4.2.
    7. Examples. In this section we give examples with two linkage classes that illustrate the
limitations of the usage of V (or its variant) as a Lyapunov function.
   7.1. An example with two linkage classes, where V does not work at the origin.
Consider the (time-independent) mass-action system
                2              1                8            1
        3X           2X + Y          X + 2Y        3Y  4X         4X + Y,
                8              1                2            1
which results in the ODE
                     ẋ = f1 (x, y) = −2x3 + 7x2 y − 7xy 2 + 2y 3 ,
                     ẏ = f2 (x, y) = +2x3 − 7x2 y + 7xy 2 − 2y 3 + x4 − x4 y.


   For (x∗ , y ∗ ) ∈ R2+ , let us define V(x∗ ,y∗ ) : R2≥0 → R≥0 , the Horn-Jackson function centered
around (x∗ , y ∗ ), by
                                                                   
                                     x                        y
        V(x∗ ,y∗ ) (x, y) = x log ∗ − 1 + x + y log ∗ − 1 + y ∗ for (x, y) ∈ R2≥0 .
                                                    ∗
                                    x                         y
PERMANENCE OF MASS-ACTION SYSTEMS                                                               11


Then the time derivative of V(x∗ ,y∗ ) along trajectories is
                                                                         
                                      f1 (x, y)        x       y    f1 (x, y)
             (grad V(x∗ ,y∗ ) )(x, y)            = log ∗ , log ∗                =
                                      f2 (x, y)        x       y    f2 (x, y)
                                                              
                         x                        y        x                   y
              =− y−             (y − x)(y − 2x) log ∗ − log ∗ + x4 (1 − y) log ∗ .
                          2                        y         x                   y

Thus, for each (x∗ , y ∗ ) ∈ R2+ , every neighborhood of the origin contains (x, y) ∈ R2+ for which
the above expression is positive. Thus, the function V(x∗ ,y∗ ) cannot serve as a Lyapunov
function close to the origin.
    On the other hand, since every planar reversible mass-action system is permanent (see
[17]), the example of this subsection is permanent.
    7.2. An example with two linkage classes, where V does not work at infinity. Consider
the (time-independent) mass-action system
                    2               1               8                1
            3X          2X + Y           X + 2Y         3Y       0        Y,
                    8               1               2                1
which results in the ODE

                       ẋ = f1 (x, y) = −2x3 + 7x2 y − 7xy 2 + 2y 3 ,
                       ẏ = f2 (x, y) = +2x3 − 7x2 y + 7xy 2 − 2y 3 + 1 − y.


    With V(x∗ ,y∗ ) : R2≥0 → R≥0 being the same function as in subsection 7.1, the time derivative
of V(x∗ ,y∗ ) along trajectories is
                                                                           
                                       f1 (x, y)         x       y    f1 (x, y)
               (grad V(x∗ ,y∗ ) )(x, y)            = log ∗ , log ∗                =
                                       f2 (x, y)         x       y    f2 (x, y)
                                                                
                           x                        y        x                  y
                =− y−             (y − x)(y − 2x) log ∗ − log ∗ + (1 − y) log ∗ .
                            2                        y         x                 y

Thus, for each (x∗ , y ∗ ) ∈ R2+ and for each M > 0 there exists (x, y) with x ≥ M , y ≥ M for
which the above expression is positive. Thus, the function V(x∗ ,y∗ ) cannot serve as a Lyapunov
function around infinity.
    On the other hand, since every planar reversible mass-action system is permanent (see
[17]), the example of this subsection is permanent.
    7.3. An example, which is complex balanced. Consider a modification of [13, Example
9.6], namely, the (time-independent) mass-action system
                                  1
                             X          Y
                                                       1
                               1      1         2X       3Y,
                                                       1
                                 Y+Z
12                                                                          B. BOROS AND J. HOFBAUER


which results in the ODE

                               ẋ = f1 (x, y, z) = −x + yz − 2x2 + 2y 3 ,
                               ẏ = f2 (x, y, z) = +x − yz + 3x2 − 3y 3 ,
                               ż = f3 (x, y, z) = +y − yz.

The point (1, 1, 1) is the unique positive equilibrium. Furthermore, this point is a complex
balanced equilibrium, and thus, according to the Global Attractor Conjecture [7], which is
proven for the three species case (see [8] and [16]), it is globally asymptotically stable, and
therefore the system is permanent. However, as we demonstrate below, the method of the
present paper fails to prove permanence.
    The set of boundary equilibria consists of the points (0, 0, z) with z ≥ 0. For (x∗ , y ∗ ) ∈ R2+ ,
let us define V(x∗ ,y∗ ) : R3≥0 → R≥0 by
                                                             
                                    x                    y
       V(x∗ ,y∗ ) (x, y, z) = x log ∗ − 1 + x + y log ∗ − 1 + y ∗ for (x, y, z) ∈ R3≥0 .
                                             ∗
                                   x                    y
Then the time derivative of V(x∗ ,y∗ ) along trajectories is
                                                                                       
                                      f1 (x, y, z)                      f1 (x, y, z)
                                                           x        y
        (grad V(x∗ ,y∗ ) )(x, y, z)  f2 (x, y, z)  = log ∗ , log ∗ , 0  f2 (x, y, z)  =
                                                          x        y
                                      f3 (x, y, z)                          f3 (x, y, z)
                                                             3                   !
                              y          x                       y           x 2
         = (x − yz) log ∗ − log ∗ + (x2 − y 3 ) log                    − log ∗          .
                              y         x                        y∗            x

Thus, for each z > 0 and for each (x∗ , y ∗ ) ∈ R2+ , every neighborhood of (0, 0, z) contains
(x, y, z) ∈ R3+ for which the above expression is positive. Thus, the function V(x∗ ,y∗ ) cannot
serve as a Lyapunov function close to (0, 0, z) with z > 0. The method in [2] therefore cannot
be extended in a straightforward manner to systems with multiple linkage classes.
